questions.question: Fill in the blank: Probability of an event E + Probability of the event 'not E' = ____.
questions.explanation: E and 'not E' are complementary, so their probabilities add up to 1.
option_feedback: No probability adds up to more than 1 here.
That is true only when both are equally likely.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The probability of an event that cannot happen is ____. Such an event is called ____.
questions.explanation: No outcome is favourable, so the probability is 0: an impossible event.
option_feedback: That is for an event that is certain.
The value 0 is right, but the event is impossible.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The probability of an event that is certain to happen is ____. Such an event is called ____.
questions.explanation: Every outcome is favourable, so the probability is 1: a sure (certain) event.
option_feedback: That is for an event that cannot happen.
The value 1 is right, but the event is sure.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is ____.
questions.explanation: Together the elementary events cover every outcome, so their probabilities add up to 1.
option_feedback: Each probability is a fraction; together they make 1.
Together they cover every outcome, so the sum is 1.

questions.question:
Which of the following experiments have equally likely outcomes? Explain.

(i) A driver attempts to start a car. The car starts or does not start.

(ii) A player attempts to shoot a basketball. She/he shoots or misses the shot.

(iii) A trial is made to answer a true-false question. The answer is right or wrong.

(iv) A baby is born. It is a boy or a girl.
answer_steps: (i) Not equally likely: a car usually starts; it depends on its condition.
(ii) Not equally likely: it depends on the player's skill.
(iii) Equally likely: a right or a wrong answer is equally possible when guessed.
(iv) Equally likely: a boy and a girl are (taken to be) equally likely.

questions.question: Why is tossing a coin considered to be a fair way of deciding which team should get the ball at the beginning of a football game?
answer_steps: Head and tail are equally likely outcomes, each with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
So neither team has an advantage: the result cannot be predicted or favoured.

questions.question: A die is thrown twice. What is the probability that (i) 5 will not come up either time? (ii) 5 will come up at least once?

Which of the following arguments are correct and which are not correct? Give reasons for your answer.

(i) If two coins are tossed simultaneously there are three possible outcomes: two heads, two tails or one of each. Therefore, for each of these outcomes, the probability is $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

(ii) If a die is thrown, there are two possible outcomes: an odd number or an even number. Therefore, the probability of getting an odd number is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
answer_steps: (i) Incorrect. The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT; 'one of each' happens in 2 ways, so its probability is $\dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
(ii) Correct. Odd (1, 3, 5) and even (2, 4, 6) each have 3 of the 6 outcomes.

questions.question:
On a particular day, Vidhi and Unnati couldn't decide on who would get to drive the car. They had one coin each and flipped their coin exactly three times. The following was agreed upon:

1. If Vidhi gets two heads in a row, she would drive the car.

2. If Unnati gets a head immediately followed by a tail, she would drive the car.

Who has greater probability to drive the car that day? Justify your answer.
answer_steps: Each has 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.
Vidhi: HHH, HHT, THH, so $P = \dfrac{3}{8}$. Unnati: HHT, HTH, HTT, THT, so $P = \dfrac{4}{8}$.

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red and 3 green balls. A ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is not green.
answer_steps: Total $= 8$; balls that are not green $= 5$.

questions.question: Find the probability that a leap year, selected at random, has 53 Sundays.
answer_steps: A leap year has 366 days $= 52$ weeks and 2 extra days. The 2 extra days can be (Sun, Mon), (Mon, Tue), …, (Sat, Sun): 7 ways.
Two of these contain a Sunday, so $P = \dfrac{2}{7}$.

A number is chosen at random from the numbers 1 to 30. Find the probability that it is (i) a prime number; (ii) a multiple of 3 or 5.
answer_steps: (ii) Multiples of 3: 10; of 5: 6; of both (15, 30): 2. So $10 + 6 - 2 = 14$ numbers.

questions.question: Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that (i) the product of the numbers is even; (ii) the sum is a multiple of 3; (iii) the sum is a prime number; (iv) both show the same number; (v) the difference of the numbers is 2.
answer_steps: (i) The product is odd only when both are odd: $3 \times 3 = 9$ ways, so $P(\text{even}) = 1 - \dfrac{9}{36} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.question:
At a school fair, a box contains 20 cards numbered 1 to 20. A player draws one card at random.

(i) Find the probability that the number is even. (1)

(ii) Find the probability that the number is prime. (1)

(iii) Find the probability that the number is a multiple of 3 or 4. OR Find the probability that the number is a perfect square. (2)
answer_steps: (iii) Multiples of 3: 6; of 4: 5; of both (12): 1, so 10 numbers: $\dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. OR 1, 4, 9, 16: $\dfrac{4}{20} = \dfrac{1}{5}$.
